sources: Ralph Wiggum Showdown with Geoffrey Huntley (2026-01-03, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SB6cO97tfiY)
sample_quote: "swallow all test/build/lint output and replace it with a single ✓ if the stage passes" (C1575)
landing_guesses: run_silent wrapper script named in CLAUDE.md Commands | pytest -x / jest --bail inner loop, full run before PR | Failure-output filters for pytest/Vitest/Jest/ruff/mypy

reviews.lens: benefit
reviews.existing_mechanism: pytest -rs skip-aware gates; capped workflow outputs (but no gate-output wrapper)
reviews.measurement: Add a run_silent wrapper (pass prints one tick, fail prints filtered output, full log goes to a file) for the gate commands in one phase; count the tokens of gate output in the transcript and the gate re-runs against the previous phase; adopt if gate tokens fall by at least 50% with no failure missed.
reviews.reason: The cheapest lever on L2 here: Docker pytest, mypy and Jest output currently lands raw in the context of a session that must last a whole phase.

reviews.lens: Cost, risk and novelty: what the harness already does (ship plan §0, ORCHESTRATION-DESIGN §3-§5, HARNESS-REVIEW §4/§6), whether a deliberate skip is re-opened, and what a one-developer Windows repo pays to build and keep it honest.
reviews.existing_mechanism: ORCHESTRATION §5: gate runners return tails + exit codes; outputs capped and sliced with dropped counts logged
reviews.measurement: Over 2 code phases, run the local gates through one Git Bash wrapper that prints a tick on pass and filtered fail-fast output on failure, with the full log written to a file. Count the gate-output tokens returned to the session against the unwrapped baseline, and count missed failures and extra re-runs. Adopt if tokens fall at least 80% with zero missed failures and zero extra re-runs.
reviews.reason: The context-flood mechanism fits L2/L3; a small script on Windows is cheap, but it must be shown not to hide failures before it becomes the only path.

refutation.counter_evidence:
1) The mechanism already exists and the phase routine already requires it. Ship plan §0 "Gates" says backend gates run through ORCHESTRATION-DESIGN Appendix A. That recipe's g() writes each gate's full output to /work/logs/gate-$i.log and prints only one "GATE[i cmd] EXIT=rc" line per gate. The script then greps only the GATE, SETUP and SUMMARY lines into the result, and the agent reports "the tail of each failing gate's log". That is run_silent, already deterministic. ORCHESTRATION §5 "Output discipline" adds: "command agents redirect npm/pytest/docker output to scratchpad logs and return tails + exit codes". S-07a node-gates "Logs to the scratchpad, reports tails". G4-A's premise ("Docker pytest, mypy and Jest output currently lands raw in the context") is therefore false for the Docker gates.
2) The L2 benefit is mostly illusory. Fable "never implements" (§0 Routing), so gate runs happen in short-lived command or implementer subagents, not in the session that must last the whole phase.
3) The scale does not carry over. This repo has 18 web test files, 39 mobile test files and 692 backend tests (pytest -q prints dots). tsc, eslint and ruff print almost nothing when they pass. Nothing here resembles C1254's 4,000 lines or C1575's monorepo.
4) A one-tick pass removes a signal the harness depends on. pyproject addopts is "-ra", the gates are skip-aware, and the §0 reviewer must list "new skip or xfail". A bare tick hides "N skipped", so an @integration run where every test skipped would look green.
5) Fail-fast (C1582) conflicts with g()'s deliberate design: "always returns 0 so every gate runs". It would also cause the extra re-runs that C1522 itself says are costly.
6) Every card is anecdotal or asserted, with no numbers. C1849 (MCP output) and C1886 (clearing earlier errors) are not about gate wrappers.
refutation.what_would_settle_it: Over the first 2 code phases that run the native web and mobile gates (lint, test, build, typecheck, jest, expo export), log for each run: the gate-output tokens that reach the main Fable session and the implementer, the number of re-runs caused because a returned tail cut off the first error (mypy/tsc/eslint list errors top-down), and whether each runner's pass/skip count appeared in the returned line. Adopt the extension only if native-gate output reaching Fable exceeds about 10k tokens in a phase, or at least one re-run happened because of a truncated tail. Otherwise skip it. In both cases, require zero gate results that hide a skip count.
refutation.reason: The core idea, a deterministic wrapper that writes full logs to a file and returns one line per gate, is already done: Appendix A's g() is mandated for backend gates by ship plan §0. The one-tick output would erase the skip-aware signal, and fail-fast contradicts the every-gate design. Only a small version survives as a trial: apply the same g() discipline (one EXIT line plus the runner's pass/skip counts, a failure excerpt instead of a bare tail) to the natively run web and mobile gates, run by the command subagent rather than Fable.

label: Models habitually pipe output through head/tail/grep, miss the failure and re-run slow suites; enforce output limits in scripts by construction, plus one CLAUDE.md line telling the model not to truncate itself.
strongest_evidence: anecdotal: example of bun test piped to head then re-run into grep; '5,000 token' figure illustrative (C1064, C1065).
sample_quote: "Now your only job is to convince the model not to do its own truncation." (C1585)
landing_guesses: Wrapper writes full output to file, prints capped summary plus path | One short universal CLAUDE.md line on running checks via the wrapper | Cap tool output by construction

reviews.lens: benefit
reviews.measurement: Bundle with the F157 trial: count head/tail/grep-piped gate runs followed by a re-run in the trial phase versus the previous phase; adopt the one-line rule only if re-runs fall.
reviews.reason: Only worth a CLAUDE.md line if the wrapper trial shows self-truncation re-runs actually happen; otherwise it is W1 bloat.

reviews.lens: Cost, risk and novelty: what the harness already does (ship plan §0, ORCHESTRATION-DESIGN §3-§5, HARNESS-REVIEW §4/§6), whether a deliberate skip is re-opened, and what a one-developer Windows repo pays to build and keep it honest.
reviews.measurement: Folded into the F157 trial: also count how often the session pipes gate output through head, tail or grep and then re-runs. The CLAUDE.md line ships only if F157 is adopted and that count is above zero.
reviews.reason: Depends on F157; a CLAUDE.md line would worsen W1, so it waits for evidence of the self-truncation pattern.

refutation.counter_evidence: (1) The harness already caps gate output by construction, on the one suite slow enough for a re-run to cost anything. In ORCHESTRATION-DESIGN-2026-10.md Appendix A (lines 630-666), the g() function writes each gate's full output to /work/logs/gate-$i.log and prints only `GATE[...] EXIT=` lines. The script then filters the log with `grep -E "^(GATE|SETUP|SUMMARY)"`, so the grep is done by the script, not chosen by the model, and the full log stays on disk. The brief tells the agent to report every GATE line plus the tail of each failing gate's log, from the file, which needs no re-run. Ship plan §0 lines 57-60 make Appendix A the required path for backend gates. Web and mobile gates run natively; they are Vitest/Jest suites that take seconds, not the five-minute bun suite in C1064. (2) There is no evidence that the CLAUDE.md line works. C1585's card says "Suggests shouting in claude.md; no measure." C1064 says the habit persists even after output is offloaded automatically. C1065's 5,000-token figure is labelled illustrative. The line would add to W1, a file already about twice the length at which adherence falls. (3) The pattern does not show up in this user's sessions. A full-text search of all transcripts, archived included, found 0 hits for "pytest -q 2>&1 | tail" and 0 for "npm test 2>&1 | tail". "2>&1 | tail" hit once, in a different project (24_Clinic_Workshop), where it failed with CommandNotFound because PowerShell, the primary shell here, has no head or tail. (4) On this machine the PowerShell tool description already tells the model to use Select-Object instead of head/tail, and both shell tools cap output at 30,000 characters. A line written around head/tail is therefore partly aimed at the wrong shell. (5) Both reviewers rated evidence 1 and benefit 1, and both made the line depend on F157 and on a pattern being observed. The transcript search above is that observation, and it came back empty.
refutation.what_would_settle_it: Reopen only on evidence, at no cost. After the first 5 ship-plan phase sessions (P1 onward), search the FixFlow transcripts for any gate command (pytest, npm test, npm run typecheck, jest, vitest, ruff, mypy) piped through head, tail, grep, Select-Object or Select-String and followed by a re-run of the same gate in the same session. Consider a CLAUDE.md line, or better a line in the gate brief, only if there are at least 3 such re-runs across those 5 sessions. Otherwise the line stays out.
refutation.reason: The by-construction cap already exists for the only slow suite (ORCHESTRATION-DESIGN Appendix A writes each gate to a log file and prints GATE/EXIT lines). The remaining piece, a CLAUDE.md line, has no measured benefit, adds to W1, and targets a habit that does not appear in this user's transcripts. Drop it.

refutation.counter_evidence: 1) The harness already applies the principle to its black boxes as phase steps, so a separate mechanism isn't needed. SHIP-PLAN §0 standing rule 2 says "No field-reliability claim without device evidence from the phone models in the fleet". P5-spike (SHIP-PLAN l.764-781) exists "to settle HR-A1b's open question with device evidence instead of a desk opinion". P3c preflight (l.626-650) checks the Cloudflare Tunnel and the CSP from the box, runs "one selfie presign → PUT → commit", and measures p50/p95 latency from a phone, with "every test has a result". P9-0b (l.1108-1121) is the Odoo "decide-before-build gate": a test company on the l10n_pk chart, a real week imported twice and update-not-duplicate checked by hand. P10b repeats that. P2c is the APK install proof. P0a lists the R2 bucket and dumps through the pooler. Those are exactly the three dependencies G4-B's trial names (VPS/Tunnel, R2 signed URLs, Odoo). Each already has a proof step, so a trial cannot credit a "learning test" with any catch the existing step would not also make. 2) The absence-report member (C1428) is already covered. ORCHESTRATION-DESIGN §5 (l.324-328, 772) says REFUTED needs positive counter-evidence and anything else is UNVERIFIABLE. l.602 says absence from introspect is "not a contradiction". l.603 settles Expo facts from the pinned sources in .fixflow-cache/expo-src rather than from docs. HARNESS-REVIEW l.32/238 keeps "code-level" separate from "device-unverified" (O01-F20) and sends device checks to P5c. 3) G4-A's trial targets facts that are being retired or were never model assertions. The ship plan takes the final Supabase dump in P0a and moves off Railway, so tests for "pooler IPv4" and "railway up from root" would test systems being shut down, and its "≥1 of 5 drifts" adopt rule is met almost by default. The eas.json empty-DSN and Sentry-plugin traps were learned from real failed builds (CLAUDE.md: "each one has already cost real time"), not from model assertions. Re-proving them costs EAS build quota, and keeping them true is the job of a repo guard, not a learning test. The harness already has that pattern: the P1 CI check that CLAUDE.md's Alembic head matches the chain, and the P13c path check turned fatal. 4) Neither the evidence nor the fit holds up. The evidence is anecdotal ("probably a hundred", with no rate of catches). In the live demo all 7 tests passed on the first run, which shows they are cheap to write, not that they pay off. The family does nothing for W2 (it does not make compliance observable) or W3 (P1's cold-resume trial already tests the routine itself). For W4/W5 it would mean authoring yet another artifact.
refutation.what_would_settle_it: Reopen only on this check: at the close of P3c, P5-spike and P9-0b, count design-relevant facts about an external system that the phase assumed from docs or a model, that its proof step did not exercise, and that later broke an implementation phase. If there is at least 1 across those three phases, run G4-B's trial on the next untested dependency. If there are 0, the skip stands.
refutation.reason: For every dependency the reviewers named, the ship plan already proves behaviour by running it before building on it: standing rule 2, P5-spike, P3c preflight, the P9-0b/P10b Odoo rehearsals, P2c and P0a. The refuter rules already treat absence as not-evidence. What would be new, saved out-of-suite test code re-run on upgrades, has no measurable counterfactual here, and G4-A's targets are being retired or are better kept as repo guards.

refutation.counter_evidence: (1) The two cards contradict each other. C1085 says low effort is enough for planned work. That is Dex's own use of GPT-5.5 on low, he admits he "has not yet formed a feel for higher effort levels", and the thousand-tests story is second-hand. C0954, a HumanLayer changelog line, removed a forced-low implementer and made it inherit the parent's effort. So the family's own evidence argues against "default low for settled plans". Even then, the release note gives no reason or numbers; "low was too weak" is the reader's inference. (2) The harness already sets implementer effort explicitly. Ship plan §0 "Routing (design doc §3)" (SHIP-PLAN-2026-11.md lines 47-50) sends invariant-sensitive code to Opus and well-specified work to Sonnet. ORCHESTRATION-DESIGN §3 (lines 88-97) sets Sonnet at medium for "straightforward implementation later" and Opus at high, with the rule "raise effort on the current tier before moving up a tier". The workflow skeleton passes `effort: t.effort` on every agent call (line 226), so the inherit-vs-forced-low problem in C0954 cannot arise. No implementer runs at low (no C0954 failure) or at xhigh (no C1085 over-testing). (3) Over-testing is already bounded by design: Sonnet writes "tests from a design's test list" (ship plan line 50). (4) G4-A's trial measures refuter effort at medium vs xhigh. That is the verifier-effort question for L1 and the SlopCodeBench family (F187), not implementer effort, so it does not support this family. G4-B is right.
refutation.reason: Implementer effort is already set per task (Sonnet medium, Opus high, via ship plan §0 → ORCHESTRATION-DESIGN §3). The cards contradict each other and are anecdotal (GPT-5.5). Verifier effort belongs to the F187 trial.

reviews.lens: Cost, risk and novelty: what the harness already does (ship plan §0, ORCHESTRATION-DESIGN §3-§5, HARNESS-REVIEW §4/§6), whether a deliberate skip is re-opened, and what a one-developer Windows repo pays to build and keep it honest.
reviews.existing_mechanism: P1 cold-resume trial with ten frozen facts; register items with known root causes and SHAs (#162 carry-in loop, unseeded dispatcher cursor)
reviews.measurement: Freeze 3 closed register defects as base SHA + neutral prompt + answer key. Use them as the fixture set in the F187 effort trial, run once at medium and once at xhigh. Keep the set only if the two runs differ on at least 1 fixture, since a set that cannot tell settings apart is not worth keeping.
reviews.reason: A cheap answer-key benchmark built from our own paid-for defects gives the L1 decision real evidence, without re-opening the M00-M06 pipeline.

refutation.counter_evidence: (1) The source data works against the family. C1019 says one race-condition case was re-run on each new model for about six months, and C0994 says Fable 5 still failed it. Every model failed, so it never told one model from another and changed no recorded decision. That is anecdotal and gives no discrimination. (2) The same video contradicts the method. In C0995 Dex says "one shot problem is like less of a useful evaluation of the gap in quality", yet both reviews propose one-shot runs. (3) Both keep rules accept noise. G4-A keeps the set if it "separates the configurations by at least 1 case" and G4-B keeps it if two single runs "differ on at least 1 fixture". With one run per configuration, a one-fixture difference is expected from run-to-run variance alone. (4) A standing "re-run on every new model" benchmark has almost nothing to decide here. ORCHESTRATION-DESIGN-2026-10.md §3 (lines 88-98) fixes model tiers by role, and models change when Anthropic releases them. The only live decision is L1 effort routing. (5) G4-A's source is wrong. docs/program/evidence/README.md says the folder holds raw W1/W2 discovery outputs, "not state", not adjudicated diagnoses tied to pre-fix SHAs. The usable answer keys are the closed defects CLAUDE.md records: #162 blank-form bill wipe, 0043 settled-job reopen, 0046 unseeded dispatcher cursor, the compare_secret TypeError, and the bill-freeze resubmit. (6) The answers can leak. This repo runs agents in .claude/worktrees, which share the object store and refs, so an agent at a pre-fix SHA can read the fix commit with git log. Each fixture needs a git-archive export, and on Windows clones need core.longpaths. Not counter-evidence, for the record: this does not re-open the M00-M06 skip in HARNESS-REVIEW §4. That skip covered a telemetry collector and run schema, and the clinic file workflow-measurement-expansion/task.md:41 shows no coding benchmark was ever run. The "owner priority low" reason still holds against any standing measurement infrastructure. The P1 cold-resume trial (SHIP-PLAN P1 Entry) tests whether a fresh agent can recover state from the docs, not model capability, so it is not a duplicate.
refutation.what_would_settle_it: A one-time run inside the L1 effort trial. Build 5 fixtures from the closed CLAUDE.md defects (#162, 0043, 0046, compare_secret, bill freeze). Each fixture is a git-archive export of the pre-fix SHA, a 2-3 sentence symptom prompt that leaves out post-fix docs, and a binary answer key naming the root-cause mechanism and file. Run every fixture 3 times on Opus at medium and 3 times at xhigh: 30 runs. Fable grades each run against its key without knowing the effort level, and records tokens per run. Keep the set as a reusable L1/model-change instrument only if all three hold: (a) xhigh solves between 1 and 4 of the 5 fixtures, so there is no floor or ceiling effect; (b) on each fixture, at least 2 of the 3 runs within a configuration agree; (c) total solves differ between configurations by 3 or more out of 15. Otherwise use the result once for the L1 decision and discard the set.
refutation.reason: The standing "week-cost journal re-run on every new model" is refuted by its own source: the one reported case never told models apart, and Dex says one-shot is a poor test in the same video. A smaller version survives as a trial: about 5 known-answer fixtures from FixFlow's closed defects, run repeatedly with blind grading as the fixture set of the L1 effort trial, with no standing infrastructure and with the reviewers' noise-prone keep rule fixed.

refutation.counter_evidence: 1) The plan half is already in place. In SHIP-PLAN-2026-11.md §0 (lines 31-32), Scope is a checkbox list. Every phase ends with a "Backlog in these files" line. For P1 (line 382) it reads "none (O05-15 → P7a; O05-17 → P0a 13)", and other phases have similar lines at 419, 456, 580, 974 and 1020; each one lists findings in the touched files that are explicitly deferred. "Size" lines also name what moves out (line 378-381: the "deep-health exposure bullet ... moves to P3a", "never cherry-picked onto release/drain"). The draft-PR journal already keeps "ruled out" entries (§0 line 39). Fable or the owner writes these plans, not the implementing model, so adding a "Not doing" line to 40 frozen phases is churn on Plan @ sha. 2) The card evidence is anecdotal only. C1373 lists the author's practice with no counts. C1770 rests on HN commenters' impressions, and its 10k-vs-200k figure is a guess. C1845 is one live plan review. 3) Transfer risk. CLAUDE.md protects code that looks like over-engineering: the outbox "Don't 'simplify' this away", the login lock "do not 'fix' this", compare_secret being total over all inputs, and "None means unknown ... never treat it as zero". An unscoped "where did you over-engineer / impossible-case handling" prompt points the reviewer at that load-bearing defensive code. 4) The review-side gap is real. The §0 reviewer brief (lines 51-55) covers register ids, fail-before/pass-after, changed expected values, removed assertions and skips, and nothing about a diff that goes beyond Scope. A grep for over-engineer, scope creep, simplify, non-goal or out of scope across pr182/docs found no such check.
refutation.what_would_settle_it: Add one line to the Opus PR-reviewer brief. It asks the reviewer to list every change in the diff that no Scope checkbox requires: unrequested abstractions, config where a constant would do, and new error branches with no Scope or test reason. The reviewer reports and never removes, and constructs named in CLAUDE.md invariants are excluded. Run it over the first 5 reviewed code-phase PRs (P1 onward). For each PR, count (a) items Fable accepts, meaning they produce a code change or a "ruled out" journal entry; (b) items Fable rejects as noise; (c) items that target a CLAUDE.md-invariant construct despite the exclusion. Keep the line if a >= 1 and c = 0 over the 5 PRs. Drop it if a = 0, or if b exceeds 3x a.
refutation.reason: Only the reviewer-brief half survives, as a trial. The plan-side "not doing" section already exists as the enumerated Scope, the "Backlog in these files" and Size lines, and the "ruled out" journal. The evidence is anecdotal, so B's adopt is too strong. The check must also exclude CLAUDE.md-protected defensive code, or it invites the reviewer to "simplify" invariants away.

label: Run the review as a separate step in a fresh context with a fixed list of known anti-patterns and a plan-vs-implementation deviation report, rather than buying a separate review product.
strongest_evidence: anecdotal: own practice; deviation reviewer almost always finds an added item between phases; vendor price ~$15-25 per review (C1282, C1416).
sample_quote: "a step in our workflow before we ship a PR where we do a code review" (C1282)
landing_guesses: Per-PR Opus reviewer with fixed FixFlow anti-pattern list | Explicit 'deviations from Plan @ sha' section

reviews.lens: benefit
reviews.existing_mechanism: Fresh-context Opus reviewer per PR; CLAUDE.md invariants act as an anti-pattern list; Plan @ sha line
reviews.measurement: Require the reviewer to output a 'deviations from Scope at Plan @ <sha>' list on the first 3 PRs; count deviations it reports that the decisions journal did not record; keep it if at least 1 turns up.
reviews.reason: The deviation report is the cheapest external check that the routine and plan were actually followed (W2), and the Plan @ sha anchor already exists.

reviews.lens: Cost, risk and novelty: what the harness already does (ship plan §0, ORCHESTRATION-DESIGN §3-§5, HARNESS-REVIEW §4/§6), whether a deliberate skip is re-opened, and what a one-developer Windows repo pays to build and keep it honest.
reviews.existing_mechanism: Opus reviewer in a fresh context with a refute-by-default brief naming register ids
reviews.measurement: Over the first 5 reviewed PRs, the reviewer emits a 'deviations from Plan @ <sha>' list; count the deviations Fable accepts as real (unplanned additions or omissions). Keep it if at least 1 appears in 5 PRs; drop it if zero.
reviews.reason: A plan-vs-diff deviation report is the one review lens we lack, it costs one brief section, and it makes skipped scope visible from outside (W2).

refutation.counter_evidence: Two of the family's three parts are already in place. (1) The separate fresh-context review: ship plan §0 Routing (SHIP-PLAN-2026-11.md lines 51-56) already gives every PR an Opus reviewer with a refute-by-default brief that names register ids. Its verdict is bound to the head SHA, it names a fail-before/pass-after test per id, and it lists changed expected values, removed assertions and new skips. HARNESS-REVIEW §4 line 261 adopted this, and no review product was ever planned. (2) The fixed anti-pattern list: ORCHESTRATION-DESIGN line 90 says every subagent loads CLAUDE.md (about 7.5k tokens). The reviewer therefore already reads CLAUDE.md's 'Invariants you must respect' and 'Do NOT assume' sections, which are FixFlow's own paid-for anti-pattern list. C1282 cites only Dex's generic list of about 12 items, with no counts, so it adds nothing evidenced. The one fixed list with no check behind it is HARNESS-REVIEW §4 lines 278-285 ('lessons without a mechanism': RT-02, RT-03, RT-06), and no card supports that use. (3) The plan-vs-implementation deviation report is genuinely absent. I grepped plan §0, ORCHESTRATION-DESIGN and HARNESS-REVIEW for deviat/unplanned/against the scope/diff against: nothing about a reviewer lens. Today Scope boxes are ticked by the implementer (§0 lines 31-32) and the Decisions journal is appended by the same session (lines 39-42), so both are self-reported. The evidence for the deviation lens is anecdotal: C1416 says it 'almost always finds an added item' but gives no counts. Its W2 benefit is also narrower than the reviewers claim. It checks whether the code matches the Scope and whether ticked boxes are real. It does not check routine compliance: whether the store was consulted, whether the six-question message was written, or whether OWNER-VIEW was refreshed. The reviewer has never run (W3), so adopting a new lens now is premature.
refutation.what_would_settle_it: For the first 5 code-phase PRs from P1 on, add one section to the Opus reviewer brief: 'Deviations from Scope at Plan @ <sha>'. It lists, each with file:line: (a) diff hunks or files that no Scope box accounts for, (b) boxes ticked with no matching diff or test, (c) unticked boxes. Fable labels each item real or noise and checks it against the PR's Decisions journal. Adopt if all three hold across the 5 PRs: at least 1 real deviation that the journal did not record (an unrecorded addition, or a ticked box with nothing behind it); noise is at most 50% of the items; and every named register id still gets its fail-before/pass-after (no crowd-out). Drop if no real unrecorded deviation turns up in 5 PRs.
refutation.reason: The fresh-context reviewer and the anti-pattern list already exist (§0 Routing; CLAUDE.md invariants, loaded by every subagent). Only the one-section deviation report against Plan @ sha survives: it is the one outside check on ticked boxes and unrecorded additions. It runs as a trial rather than an adopt because its evidence is anecdotal and the reviewer has never run.

label: Not every PR needs a max-effort reviewer: vendor review on every PR is expensive when most do not need that rigour, so risk-tier the reviewer.
strongest_evidence: asserted: Vaibhav's argument with loose ~$25/PR figure (C1283).
sample_quote: "most PRs don't need that level of rigor" (C1283)
landing_guesses: Risk-tier the reviewer; not every PR needs a max-effort refuter

reviews.lens: benefit
reviews.existing_mechanism: Every PR gets an Opus reviewer regardless of risk (ship plan §0)
reviews.measurement: For the first 4 docs-only or infra-only PRs (no Opus-owned paths), run both a Sonnet/medium reviewer and the Opus reviewer on the same head SHA; compare findings the owner accepts and cost; tier those PRs down if Sonnet misses no accepted finding.
reviews.reason: Tiering reviewer cost by risk is the clearest L1 saving, and the routing list already defines the high-risk paths.

reviews.lens: Cost, risk and novelty: what the harness already does (ship plan §0, ORCHESTRATION-DESIGN §3-§5, HARNESS-REVIEW §4/§6), whether a deliberate skip is re-opened, and what a one-developer Windows repo pays to build and keep it honest.
reviews.existing_mechanism: ORCHESTRATION §3: Opus at high, xhigh for skeptics and the geofence analyst; every PR gets the same Opus reviewer
reviews.measurement: On the next 3 non-invariant PRs, run the reviewer twice at the same head SHA, once at medium and once at xhigh, blind to each other and with the F181 fixtures included. Count the findings Fable accepts and the correct fail-before/pass-after namings from each. Move non-invariant PRs to medium if medium misses zero accepted findings and costs at least 30% fewer tokens; invariant-sensitive PRs stay at xhigh either way.
reviews.reason: L1's actual decision: the SlopCodeBench medium-vs-xhigh result was measured on a different task, so test it on our own PRs before changing the effort level.

refutation.counter_evidence: (1) The premise misreads the harness. Ship plan §0 Routing (SHIP-PLAN-2026-11.md line 51) says which model reviews ("an Opus reviewer") but sets no effort level, and the plan never uses "xhigh" or "effort" anywhere. ORCHESTRATION-DESIGN §3 (line 97) sets Opus to `high` by default and keeps `xhigh` for the geofence analyst and the P0 skeptics. Its routing rule (line 88) says "raise effort on the current tier before moving up a tier". So the harness has no "max-effort reviewer on every PR" to tier down. (2) The plan already scopes review by risk. P7b-2 (line 1051) is "Sonnet; Opus reviews media", P3a (line 573) is "Opus reviews compose, restore order", and P5d-2 (line 926) is "Sonnet tabulates; the session judges". Each reviewer brief also lists only the register ids it must try to break. (3) Almost no PRs are eligible. Of the ~32 phase Workflow lines, only four are Sonnet-implemented code PRs: P3a, P7b-2, P12 and P13c. Every other code phase touches the §0 Opus-owned list (outbox, lifecycle, money or ledger, auth or PIN, migrations, native patches, location bounds). Both proposed trials ("first 4 docs-only/infra PRs" in A, "next 3 non-invariant PRs" in B) would use up that whole group, and doubling the reviewer on those PRs would cost more than tiering could save afterwards. Docs and config PRs also have small diffs, so an Opus review of them is already cheap. (4) Those few PRs are exactly the ones Sonnet writes. For them the Opus reviewer is the only check from a stronger model than the author's, and the only verification besides CI that is not self-reported (W2). Swapping in a Sonnet reviewer would leave the weaker author checked by the same tier. (5) The evidence is one asserted card. C1283 quotes "about $25 per PR quoted loosely; no data", and the argument is mostly Vaibhav's. It concerns paid vendor review services, which bill per PR; here the reviewer is a subagent paid from subscription usage. Dex's agreement in that card is about the writing agent getting it right first time, not about reviewer tiers. His L3 line, "no software factory without better verifiers", points the other way.
refutation.what_would_settle_it: Re-open only if the plan changes. Recount the ship plan's Workflow lines that are code PRs off the §0 Opus-owned list (there are 4 today: P3a, P7b-2, P12, P13c). If a re-plan pushes that count above about 10, run G4-B's medium-vs-high comparison on 3 of them.
refutation.reason: The harness already scopes review by risk (P3a, P7b-2) and sets Opus to high by default (§3), not maximum effort. Only about 4 plan PRs are low-risk, and the trial would use all of them, so the saving is illusory. The one leftover is a one-clause note in §0 saying the reviewer runs at the §3 default, and that needs no trial.

refutation.counter_evidence: (1) HumanLayer's dollar figures don't apply here. get_usage on 2026-11-04 shows the account is on a flat "Ultra" subscription with extra usage disabled, so a phase costs nothing extra in dollars. The limit that actually binds is the weekly usage window (all models 64% used, Fable 71% used, 5 days before reset). The harness has already hit that limit: HARNESS-REVIEW-2026-11-01.md line 7 says 7 refuters were "lost to a usage limit", and line 210 says seven A4b/A4c refuter runs never happened. The $12k/month, $650 for two PRs and $10-11/hour figures come from pay-per-use API credits. (2) The members are weak evidence. C1795 is one self-reported figure with "no breakdown". C1812 has "no figure stated". C1699 says "cost not quantified". C1374 is a rough hackathon estimate. C1767's critics point to 40 commits over 7 days and a PR still in draft. None of them splits spend by role, so none supports a verifier-share threshold. (3) Neither reviewer's measurement can come from the tools they name. get_usage returns only weekly-window percentages (all models and Fable) plus context-window size. It gives no spend per subagent, per tier or per verifier, and on a subscription /cost gives no per-agent dollars either. Splitting out "Opus reviewer/skeptic spend" means parsing subagent transcripts or workflow journal.jsonl files. That is a script, and the first step of the measurement pipeline M00-M06 that was skipped for good reason. So the line is not "one manually copied line". (4) The split would not change the decision. ORCHESTRATION-DESIGN-2026-10.md §7 already holds a cost envelope with up to 12 Opus skeptics against 7 Opus analysts, so B's trigger (over 20% in any phase) and A's (over 30% in 3 of 5) are close to certain to fire by design. (5) C1699's "stable prefix first" landing is already in place: the CONTEXT block goes first in every brief (§5.1), and the Claude Code client handles caching itself.
refutation.what_would_settle_it: Over P1-P3, record two things in the closing message's "what evidence ran" line. First, the weekly-window percentages from get_usage (all models and Fable), read at phase open and at phase close. Second, the totals each Workflow run already reports: subagent tokens, and the number of agents lost to a usage limit. Also note whether another session did heavy work during the phase; if one did, mark that phase's reading confounded. Add no tier split and write no parser. Decision rule. If any phase loses an agent to a usage limit, or one unconfounded phase uses 25% or more of the weekly all-models window (meaning fewer than 4 phases fit in a week), run the G4-F228 effort A/B on refuters, where usage-limit headroom is the outcome measured. If all three phases use under 15% each and lose no agents, close L1 as not binding. If the readings fall in between, record two more phases and apply the same rule.
refutation.reason: HumanLayer's API-credit spend figures don't apply to a flat subscription where weekly usage limits are what bind. The per-tier verifier-share line both reviewers propose can't be read from get_usage or /cost and would need a transcript parser, which is the skipped pipeline. Only a smaller trial survives: one line per phase recording the change in weekly-window percent and the workflow-reported tokens and agents lost to usage limits, gating the G4-F228 effort trial.

It works if CI fails on a deliberately planted new violation and passes on the baseline, and the baseline count only ever falls.

refutation.counter_evidence: (1) The honest-options half is already in place, and both reviewers agree. "Fix" is the PR itself. "Ignore with a recorded reason" is the Decisions / ruled out journal in ship plan §0, plus the reviewer listing every new skip or xfail with its reason. Per-id attribution is the reviewer naming, for each register id, a test that fails on base and passes on head (§0 lines 29-32). "One commit per issue" adds nothing, because PRs land as squash commits (§0 lines 43-46), so per-issue commits do not survive on main. (2) The ratchet half does not fit P5b-2. Grepping technician-app/src today finds only a handful of direct write calls from screens: JobsListScreen.tsx:156 calls jobsApi.claim, JobDetailScreen.tsx:433 and ArrivalJobBillScreen.tsx:371 call messagingApi.logSend, and features/auth/AuthContext.tsx:78 calls authApi.login. The raw-fetch rule has no violations (wifi.ts:20 is NetInfo.fetch, not fetch). With about four edges there is no wall of red CI to soften. The harness's own method already covers them: decide each edge and allow-list it with a reason. P5b-2 already allows the jobs to attendance edge "consciously" (ship plan line 864), and CLAUDE.md says "A new edge must be added to the allow-list consciously". The backend import-linter and ESLint gates block from day one, with no advisory phase. (3) A dependency-cruiser baseline works badly here. It records from-module, to-module and rule only. Screens import the whole jobsApi object and use it for reads (get) as well as writes (claim). So a baseline would freeze edges like JobsListScreen to jobsApi, and an existing screen that later adds a new jobsApi write call would pass, because no new edge appears. That is exactly the regression the rule exists to catch. (4) A baseline also contradicts the family's own "ignore with a recorded reason": it is a generated file with no reasons in it. It would also silence messagingApi.logSend, which may be a real defect: the bill-freeze invariant depends on that log landing. (5) Weakness W2 (compliance is self-reported) gets worse, not better. Nothing stops an agent that hits red CI from regenerating the baseline with --output-type baseline. Reviewer G4-B's "the baseline count only ever falls" would need a separate check that does not exist. (6) The source's "dampener" belongs to a scheduled actuator loop that keeps improving a measured count (React Doctor). FixFlow runs no such loop. The evidence is one anecdotal example with no numbers.
refutation.what_would_settle_it: In P5b-2, run the written dependency-cruiser rules once against main, with type-only imports excluded, and count the value-level violations. If there are 10 or fewer, allow-list each one with a written reason or fix it, and use no baseline; this repo is at about 4 today. Revisit a baseline only if the count is above about 20, and only together with a CI check that fails when the known-violations file grows.
refutation.reason: Skip. The honest-options half already exists (the §0 decisions journal, the reviewer's skip reasons, the per-id fail-before/pass-after test), and per-issue commits are lost to squash merges. The ratchet half solves a problem P5b-2 does not have: about 4 existing violations, better handled by the harness's reasoned allow-list. A baseline would hide new write calls on existing screen-to-jobsApi edges and add a baseline file agents can regenerate. P5b-2 should still note one finding: its "write functions" rule can't be expressed per module while screens import jobsApi as a whole, and the first run will hit the claim, logSend and login edges.

refutation.counter_evidence: (1) The generated dependency diagram (C1405) is beaten by mechanisms already in place. CLAUDE.md "Respect slice boundaries" says import-linter contracts (backend/pyproject.toml [tool.importlinter]) and ESLint no-restricted-imports are enforced in CI, so a broken boundary fails the build; a picture still needs a human to look at it. HARNESS-REVIEW-2026-11-01.md §5 and Q3 already adopted dependency-cruiser as CI import rules for mobile (P5b-2) in place of graph tooling, and the skip reason still holds: "the graph goes stale under the cherry-pick-only release branches". The BAML anecdote, a bridge importing the compiler, is exactly the class an import contract catches. (2) The per-folder HTML summaries (C0890) are secondhand ("something he saw the prior week") and sit next to a HumanLayer product feature, so they score as a claim. Phases are one per PR and already close with the six-question message plus a refreshed OWNER-VIEW.md (SHIP-PLAN §0, lines 45-47). (3) The reviewer-curated "files the owner must read" list that both reviewers converged on is AI-judged salience. The owner cannot see what it leaves out, which is W2's shape (self-reported, unverifiable from outside), so it does not help W2 and does nothing for W3. G4-B's success test ("no post-merge defect in a file the list omitted" over P1-P3) cannot be falsified at that sample size. (4) What the harness lacks: SHIP-PLAN §0 (lines 51-56) has the reviewer list every changed expected value, removed assertion and new skip/xfail, which covers weakened tests. Nothing lists changes to the files that define the gates themselves: import-linter contracts, ESLint restricted imports, ci.yml, test-runner config, the line-368 negative-mention allow-list, CLAUDE.md invariants. Per OWNER-VIEW.md, "You merge every PR". C1407's actual claim is about these boundary or verifier-defining files ("you don't generally want to automate the checking of this file").
refutation.what_would_settle_it: For the first 5 code-phase PRs, the Opus reviewer verdict adds a "gate-file changes" list. It is produced mechanically: `git diff --name-only <base>..<head>` filtered against a fixed path set (backend/pyproject.toml importlinter/ruff/mypy/pytest sections, the ESLint config, .github/workflows/ci.yml, jest/vitest/pytest config, the dependency-cruiser config once P5b-2 lands, the negative-mention allow-list, CLAUDE.md). Each hunk gets a one-line why. The owner reads only those hunks before merging and records two things in the PR journal: minutes spent, and whether any entry changed the merge decision or produced an owner correction. Count three things: (a) whether the reviewer's list matches the mechanical filter, with the target being 5/5 PRs; (b) owner minutes per PR, with the target ≤5; (c) list entries that led to a decision or correction. Keep the list if (a) is 5/5 and either (c) ≥1 or the owner rates it useful at the P5 retrospective. Drop the reviewer-written prose if (a) misses in any PR (the plain git filter replaces it). Drop the field entirely if the owner reports it as overhead with (c)=0.
refutation.reason: The diagrams and per-folder HTML are refuted: import-linter, ESLint and the planned dependency-cruiser fail the build on a broken boundary, which is stronger than a picture, and the graphify skip reason still holds. A smaller version survives as a trial: a mechanical (not AI-curated) list of changed gate-defining files for the owner to read before the merge they already do. It extends the reviewer's existing list of removed assertions and new skips from tests to the gates themselves.

reviews.measurement: Rerun 8 committed Opus xhigh skeptic or reviewer briefs at medium (keep Opus), each against the commit its brief named, and diff the verdicts (CONFIRMED/REFUTED/UNVERIFIABLE) plus the traced path. Pass if at least 7 of 8 verdicts agree AND medium misses no CONFIRMED P0. Then move non-invariant verifiers to medium or high and keep xhigh for P0 and invariant skeptics. Otherwise keep xhigh. Run it only if G4-F203 shows verifier spend at 20% or more.
reviews.reason: This is the cheapest honest test of L1: about 8 Opus runs on a labeled set we already hold. SlopCodeBench's medium-versus-xhigh result is measured on a different task type, so it cannot be adopted untested.

refutation.counter_evidence:
(1) Both cards are weak evidence. C1340 is a recalled anecdote with no numbers. C1341 is an assertion that Dex himself hedges ("would love to be proven wrong").

(2) The harness already has the family's literal content. docs/program/evidence/README.md stores every agent output verbatim, per case, with a sha256 manifest. Nothing in the harness uses LLM-generated synthetic fixtures. The register is built from traced real code (ORCHESTRATION-DESIGN §4.2 verdict rules), and the P1 cold-resume trial uses frozen facts taken from the repository.

(3) G4-A's trial cannot be run. It needs at least 4 REFUTED cases from the committed skeptic evidence. G2-deep-dive-gate-2026-11-01.md §1.1 lists 12 Opus/xhigh skeptic verdicts: 10 CONFIRMED, the rest PARTIALLY. §1.3 says "none refuted a claim".

(4) G4-B's trial is aimed at the wrong class. ORCHESTRATION-DESIGN §3 (line 97) already sets Opus to `high` by default and uses `xhigh` only for O-01 and P0/invariant skeptics. §4.2 says "Other P1s share one Opus / high skeptic". The 12 committed skeptics are exactly the P0/invariant class that both reviewers would keep at xhigh. So a pass would change no routing decision, and the "move non-invariant verifiers to medium/high" end state is mostly in place already.

(5) The inputs are not "the same brief". The W2 evidence holds the analyst outputs (O-xx), buckets.json and web-recheck.txt, but no per-skeptic brief. No PR reviewer has run yet (W3), so a rerun would rebuild the briefs from the §4.2 template.

(6) The labels are xhigh's own verdicts, adjudicated by Fable. Scoring medium against them measures agreement with xhigh, not correctness.

(7) SlopCodeBench measured a different task type, and it is the author's own report, so it scores as a claim.
refutation.reason: Narrowed. Snapshotting outputs and avoiding synthetic fixtures is already done (evidence/README.md, §4.2), and both reviewers' trials fail on the evidence: G4-A needs REFUTED cases that do not exist (G2 §1.3), and G4-B tests the P0/invariant skeptic class that §3 keeps at xhigh. What survives is a rerun of the committed, mixed-verdict knowledge-store refuter set at high, gated on G4-F203, where xhigh is actually spent.

reviews.reason: This is the most direct W2 lever in the group: deterministic assertions on artefacts let a skipped routine show from outside, without the hooks the review declined.

reviews.lens: cost, risk and novelty: what the harness already does, whether a deliberate skip is reopened, and what a single developer on Windows would pay to build, run and keep it honest
reviews.existing_mechanism: None. Compliance is self-reported in the closing message and PR body (W2). The CI gate on CLAUDE.md's Alembic head is the nearest pattern.
reviews.reopens_skipped: Pre-commit verification hook ('RT-04/05 defects; CI gates the PRs'): not reopened. This is a CI-side PR-body check, which the skip's own reason endorses, not a local hook.
reviews.measurement: Add an advisory (non-blocking) CI job that reads github.event.pull_request.body and asserts structure: line 1 is 'Plan @ <40-hex sha>'; a 'Decisions / ruled out / owner corrections' section exists; when the PR is marked ready, a reviewer comment names the current head SHA. Run it over P1-P3. Make it blocking if it catches at least 1 routine omission the owner confirms as real, with 0 false flags. Drop it if it only ever passes or flags noise.
reviews.reason: It is cheap and the only family here that makes the routine's compliance visible from outside without a hook. It is advisory first because operations phases have no PR, and a structure check can be satisfied with hollow content.

refutation.counter_evidence: (1) The evidence does not transfer. C1827 is anecdotal and comes from another domain: BAML unit tests on a Linear agent's structured tool-choice output (about 10 tools). The phase routine produces no structured next-step-intent trace. Making one would mean hooks or transcript parsing, and the review skipped that whole class: the pre-commit hook, the context system and the M00–M06 measurement pipeline (HARNESS-REVIEW §4 rows 272, 273, 275). (2) Where the harness does have structured agent outputs, it already asserts on them. Workflow subagents return JSON-schema-typed objects (ORCHESTRATION-DESIGN §5.2), the tool validates them, and Sonnet citation checks follow (ORCHESTRATION line 315). That half of the idea is already done. (3) Two of G4-A's five assertions cannot work as specified. The six-question close was adopted "as a message format, not a file" (HARNESS-REVIEW §4 line 262), so a script over gh pr view and the diff cannot see it. OWNER-VIEW.md is refreshed after the closing message (SHIP-PLAN §0 lines 43-46). That is at or after the owner's merge, and the refresh can be a no-op, so "OWNER-VIEW.md in the diff" would raise false flags. (4) G4-A's "first 3 phases (P1 included)" is mis-specified: P0a and P0b are owner sessions with no PR (SHIP-PLAN lines 219, 295). About 18 of the roughly 45 phase headings are owner or operations phases, and the ×n repeats (P4b, P4r, P5d-1a/b) mean they make up a large share of sessions. Those phases keep the Plan line and journal in W0-results.md, not in a PR body, so a PR check misses them. (5) A structure check passes hollow compliance, and a model told the format will write it. The reviewer-SHA line is also typed by Fable, so the check catches a forgotten re-review after a push, not a false one. It never shows whether the knowledge store was consulted or whether the journal was appended mid-phase.
refutation.what_would_settle_it: Put the check in a separate GitHub Actions workflow file, so that body edits do not re-run the three CI jobs. Natural home: P1-ci, which SHIP-PLAN P1 already allows for CI harness items. Run it advisory-only over the first 5 code-phase PRs (P1 or P1-ci, P2a, P2b-1, P2b-2, P3a). It asserts three things. First, line 1 matches `Plan @ <hex sha>` and that sha resolves on origin/main. Second, the "Decisions / ruled out / owner corrections" heading is present. Third, at ready-for-review and at merge, the latest posted Opus verdict comment names the current head SHA. This needs one new convention: Fable posts each verdict with gh pr comment. For each PR, count: flags raised, flags the owner confirms as a real omission, false flags, and pushes after review (merge head different from the SHA in the verdict comment). Optionally also report from the PR's GraphQL userContentEdits whether journal entries landed mid-phase or only at close; report this, never gate on it. Make the SHA assertion blocking if there is at least 1 owner-confirmed real omission and 0 false flags across the 5 PRs. Drop the whole check if there are 0 flags and 0 pushes after review across the 5 PRs, or if there are 2 or more false flags.
refutation.reason: Narrowed. The family's own idea (asserting on a structured next-step-intent trace) does not transfer: the phase routine has no such trace, a trace would need the hooks the review skipped, and the workflow-output half is already done by §5.2 schemas and citation checks. What survives is a cheap, advisory CI check on code-phase PR bodies: the Plan line, the journal heading, and a posted reviewer verdict whose SHA matches the head at merge. It drops the closing-message and OWNER-VIEW assertions, which are false-flag prone. It does not reopen the pre-commit skip, whose reason was that CI gates the PRs. Its W2 benefit is limited to a forgotten form step and a forgotten re-review after a push.

refutation.counter_evidence: 1) The evidence is zero, and neither card is about the harness. C1284 (G5-cards.md l.395) is a business-moat aside ("you can't build a company on a prompt"), evidence "Business opinion; no data". C1705 (l.539) is a co-host platitude, "counted only as Dex's framing for running the episode". Both are tagged "bears on: none". Neither proposes a mechanism, a trigger or a measure. 2) G5-A's trial (re-run the cold-resume check on a model change) is the reviewer's own invention, not something the source contains. It also fails on its own terms. (a) HARNESS-REVIEW-2026-11-01.md §4 table rules the cold-resume trial "trial once" as P1's first act. SHIP-PLAN P1 Entry (l.322-329) already says what follows from it: the main session judges the misses and fixes the plan. Whether to keep the trial depends on that unrun result (W3). (b) expected.json holds ten frozen facts "about this phase" (P1). Once P1 merges they are history, so a later re-run tests recall of a closed phase, not the routine for the current one. Keeping the check would need a newly written expected.json per phase, so it is not "almost free". (c) The pass rule "at least as many facts as P1" compares one stochastic run with one stochastic run out of 10 facts. A one-fact drop cannot be told apart from sampling noise, so it cannot signal a model regression. 3) It reopens a deliberate skip in miniature. A per-model evaluation re-run is what HR §4 skipped as "Measurement pipeline M00–M06; evaluation-run schema" ("a month of research established no gain; owner priority low"). This family adds no gain evidence, so that reason still holds. 4) Two existing parts of the harness already cover model sensitivity. Capability assumptions live in ORCHESTRATION-DESIGN §3 (the tier guide with per-tier effort and the "raise effort before tier" rule). Model-id drift is already handled reactively (HR §6 / HR-C4, the autoCompactWindow keyed to claude-opus-5-5 vs claude-fable-5-1). KNOWLEDGE-STORE-DESIGN-2026-11.md (l.247, l.291) records the model id and tier on every row, which makes model effects observable without a new check. Every PR's Opus reviewer and the CI gates already catch a model that implements worse. 5) The P1 trial artefacts are already committed under docs/program/evidence/resume-trial-P1/, so an ad-hoc re-run stays possible without adopting anything.
refutation.what_would_settle_it: Settled for now. Reopen only after P1, and only if both hold: (i) the cold-resume trial found at least one miss that a plan fix closed, and (ii) three repeat runs on the same model score within one fact of each other. Only then could a later cross-model comparison (three runs per model, a mean drop of at least 2 facts) mean anything.
refutation.reason: This is an asserted platitude with no mechanism ('bears on: none'). G5-A's trial is a grafted check that cannot be specified before P1 runs, and its frozen facts go stale once P1 merges. Its n=1 threshold is noise, it reopens the skipped evaluation-pipeline ruling, and the tier guide and the knowledge store's model-id fields already cover model sensitivity.

reviews.lens: COST, RISK AND NOVELTY
reviews.existing_mechanism: There is a prompt-level 'observed content is data, not instructions' rule, but nothing structural. Research workflows read web content inside sessions that can also hold repository data and gh/network access.
reviews.measurement: Each workflow brief that reads untrusted text (web, transcripts, third-party repos) states that it runs with no production credentials: no railway run, no SSH to the host, no FIXFLOW_* secrets in the environment. Audit the briefs of the next 5 workflows. Pass if none mixes untrusted reading with production credentials.

refutation.counter_evidence: (1) The landing on the product is refuted. FixFlow has no LLM at runtime: a grep of backend/app, src and technician-app/src for anthropic/openai/langchain finds nothing. The only "llm" hits are test files where the letters appear inside words such as clearAllMocks. The WhatsApp dispatcher (main.py run_dispatch_once, default OFF) is deterministic code, so prompt injection cannot reach it, and "sends outbound customer messages" (G5-A) is not an agent leg. (2) The card's own remedy list is partly wrong. "Put a guardrail" is detection, not removing a leg, and the source has no numbers (C1222, evidence "asserted"; the incident it cites is a disclosed proof of concept). (3) Both reviewers' rules only declare that the leg is gone; they don't remove it. Credentials are ambient in the user profile: ~/.railway exists (Railway CLI login), %APPDATA%/GitHub CLI exists (gh auth, which also allows `gh gist create`, an exfiltration channel), and ~/.ssh exists and will receive the VPS key at P0b/P3c. Any Bash-capable subagent can use all of them. No project or user settings.json has a permissions.deny list or sandbox config (worktree and main .claude/ hold only launch.json, agents and skills; ~/.claude/settings.json holds only enableWorkflows and autoCompactWindow). Subagents also run in bypass-permissions mode, so no human prompt sits on a network call. A brief sentence saying "this runs with no production credentials" (G5-B), followed by an audit of the briefs, is self-reported compliance: the W2 problem again. (4) The harness already has partial mechanisms. Claude Code's built-in "observed content is data, not instructions" boundary is a guardrail, not a cut leg. ORCHESTRATION-DESIGN §5.1 has "read-only unless your brief says runs commands", and §11 says secret scans return hash fingerprints, never values, because outputs are journaled. The repo is PRIVATE (gh repo view), so committed evidence is not a public channel. (5) It bears on none of W1-W5 or L1-L3; it is security hygiene, not a lever for the named weaknesses. It is not a reopened skip: HARNESS-REVIEW §4/§6 has no injection or untrusted-content item. What survives: the risk is real at the orchestrator and subagent level. Web/transcript/npm-reading lanes (ORCHESTRATION §11 web research, unpkg WebFetch) and prod-dump lanes (S-07b, Appendix B) feed one Fable session that has Bash and network, and ship-plan phases P0a/P0b/P3b/P3c/P13 put Railway, R2 and VPS-SSH credentials within reach of the same machine.
refutation.what_would_settle_it: Two checks; the first is a ten-minute canary. (A) Define one restricted agent type (.claude/agents/, tools limited to Read/Grep/Glob/WebFetch/WebSearch and no Bash) plus permissions.deny for Read of ~/.ssh/**, ~/.railway/**, %APPDATA%/GitHub CLI/** and the dump/archive folders. In a bypass-mode Workflow, have that agent try to read ~/.railway and ~/.ssh/known_hosts and to run ssh, railway and gh. It passes only if the harness refuses all of them; the model declining on its own does not count. Then run 3 real research briefs through the agent: pass if none drops to tool_status web_unavailable or loses facts compared with an unrestricted run. If deny rules or the agent's tool list are not enforced on workflow subagents, the structural version is dead and only a planning rule remains, which is worth skip. (B) If A passes: over the next 5 workflows or phases that read untrusted text, count from the session transcripts' tool-call logs (not from what the briefs say) any agent context that both read untrusted text (web, transcript, third-party package) and either touched a credential path, ran railway, ssh, gh gist or curl, or read a prod dump. Pass at 0, plus one SHIP-PLAN line confirmed: P0a/P0b/P3b/P3c/P13 sessions load no WebFetch/WebSearch.
refutation.reason: Narrowed. The dispatcher landing is refuted (no LLM in the product), and so is "a guardrail fixes it". The reviewers' brief-sentence rule changes nothing: Railway and GitHub CLI credentials sit in the user profile and subagents run in bypass mode. What survives is a trial of a structural cut of the private-data leg: a restricted research agent type with deny rules for any context that reads web/transcript/third-party text, plus no WebFetch/WebSearch in sessions that hold prod credentials. It is cheap, but it buys nothing on W1-W5/L1-L3, and it works only if A shows the restrictions are enforced on workflow subagents.
